name: Fatima Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time, Fatima. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can share what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew at the Westgate depot, working the city and the industrial estates. Most days we're in the bucket truck changing insulators, fitting new transformers on poles, that kind of thing. But I've also become the person for the laser scanning, LiDAR they call it, where a drone flies the line and builds a 3D picture, so we can see where trees are getting too close before they cause a fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building something that works and getting it right first time. I use AI every day, for job plans, for reading the scan results, even for sorting out the kids' after-school timetable. What wears me out is the waiting. Waiting for approvals, waiting for the outage window, waiting for someone else to finish their bit. I've been quietly writing a business plan for my own small contracting firm, because I think I could do it faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, and people who work hard still win. I'd say that at work and to my sisters on the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine by me. My job stays, Kemal's heating business stays, and I'd still have the AI helping me with the boring bits. And my contracting plan still makes sense, maybe more, because the big companies won't have changed much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving toward the firm. We've got more than a year of bills saved, plus a separate pot for a van and tools. I'd probably start the firm in two or three years, small, with one truck and a drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited, because the plan still holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the business plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Vegetation surveys and small line jobs for the utility, the bits they contract out anyway. Me, one other lineworker, a drone, a truck. I've had the AI help me cost it, line by line. Kemal says I spend more time on it than on him, which is a fair complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith or family come into a decision like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. I'd pray about it, and I'd talk to my father, who ran a grocery for thirty years. He says a business is like a child, it needs you every day. I'd not start it until Can is a bit older.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and hard workers still win, both at work and on my family group chat.
S0.think: It would suit me because my job and my husband's heating business would stay and I'd still have AI for the boring bits. My plan to start a contracting firm would make even more sense.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving toward her own firm, with over a year of bills saved plus a separate fund for a van and tools. Plans to start small, with one truck and a drone, in two or three years.
S0.feel: Calm and a little excited because her plan still holds.
S0.quote: Kemal says I spend more time on it than on him, which is a fair complaint.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima mixes daily AI use with a traditional, family-centred approach to risk. Her father's advice about running a business shapes her timing. She's already costed a contracting firm in detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people willing to work and learn. The ones who wait for someone to rescue them will struggle. Companies will need smaller, faster contractors who know the new kit, and that's where I'd want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my moment. If the utility starts using drones and AI for surveys, they'll contract a lot of it out, and I already know how to do it. The risk is that a big firm gets there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the firm forward, start it within a year. Spend the van-and-tools pot on a good drone and the scanning software, and keep my job part-time for the first six months if they'd let me. Use AI for quotes, scheduling, invoicing, the whole back office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, energised. A bit nervous about leaving a safe wage, but in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a safe wage with two kids and a mortgage. What does Kemal say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says, if you're going to do it, do it while the door's open. He's self-employed, so he knows the ups and downs. We'd agree a line: if the firm hasn't covered my wage by eighteen months, I go back to a crew. There's plenty of crews hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older men on my crew who don't touch tablets. They're good at the work, they taught me. But if the company sends a drone instead of a crew to check the line, their overtime goes first. I'd hire one of them if I could.

S1.say: I'd say this is an opportunity for people willing to work and learn, and companies will need smaller, faster contractors who know the new kit.
S1.think: This is my moment, because if the utility contracts out drone and AI surveys, I already know how to do it. The risk is a big firm getting there first.
S1.do: Starts her contracting firm within a year, spending the van-and-tools fund on a drone and scanning software. Keeps her job part-time for six months if allowed and runs the back office with AI.
S1.feel: Calm and energised, with healthy nerves about leaving a safe wage.
S1.quote: We'd agree a line: if the firm hasn't covered my wage by eighteen months, I go back to a crew.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change speeds up her business plan instead of threatening her. She has a clear fallback built on plentiful local crew jobs. She'd want to hire an older colleague whose overtime would vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big companies rushed it and the government let them. I believe in markets, but a market needs time to work. Two years isn't a market, it's a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my plan dies. If a robot can do the line work and an AI can do the planning, a small firm like mine is just a middleman. Kemal's heating jobs too, robots in people's homes by 2028. We've got savings, but I'd feel like the floor had moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shelve the firm the same week and keep my job. I'd put the van-and-tools pot into savings and some into the companies making the robots, because if they're winning, I want a piece. I'd ask to run the robot trials at Westgate, so at least I'm useful for longer. And I'd talk to the children about what they study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for food on the table, but for the future I'd planned. That plan was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elif and Can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elif's thirteen and wants to be an architect. I'd tell her to keep going, but to learn to use the AI better than anyone. Can's ten, he'd ask if the robots pray. I'd tell him no, and that's one thing that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in the robot makers while blaming the big companies. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have to like the weather to carry an umbrella. If they're going to win, my family shouldn't be the ones left with nothing. My father would say the same.

S2.say: I'd say big companies rushed it and government let them, and while I believe in markets, two years isn't a market, it's a flood.
S2.think: My business plan dies, because once robots do the line work and AI does the planning, a small firm is just a middleman. My husband's heating jobs would be hit too.
S2.do: Shelves the contracting firm within a week and keeps her job. Moves the van-and-tools fund into savings and robotics shares, asks to run the depot's robot trials and talks with her children about their studies.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about money for food but about losing the future she had planned.
S2.quote: I don't have to like the weather to carry an umbrella.
S2.fieldNote: Her anxiety is about a lost personal project, not survival, since savings are strong. She blames rushed companies while investing in them, and explained the contradiction calmly. Faith comes up as the thing machines can't share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning for anyone who's willing to move. Don't sit and complain, get ahead of it. I'd tell the younger lineworkers to learn the robots now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years changes my plan, it doesn't kill it. Instead of a firm with crews, I'd build a firm that runs robots for the utility, set-up, checking, the human on site. For three or four years, that's a real business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the firm in year one, but built around machines from the start. Buy one robot unit as soon as there's a reliable one to lease, hire one older lineworker who knows the city, use AI for everything in the office. Keep a year of bills untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but excited too. It's a short window, and I'd want to jump through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said for three or four years. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I sell the firm to a bigger one, maybe it just stops. I'd treat it like a harvest. You bring it in while it's ripe, you don't pretend it lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that feel for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy. Kemal would have to do more of the school runs. My mother would help. That's what family's for, and I'd do the same for my sisters. We'd sit down together and agree it first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning for anyone willing to move, and younger lineworkers should learn the robots now instead of complaining.
S3.think: Five years changes my plan rather than killing it, because I could build a firm that runs robots for the utility, handling set-up, checks and on-site work, for three or four years.
S3.do: Starts a robot-based contracting firm in the first year, leasing one reliable robot unit and hiring an older lineworker who knows the city. Runs the office with AI and keeps a year of bills untouched.
S3.feel: Uneasy but excited, keen to jump through a short window.
S3.quote: I'd treat it like a harvest. You bring it in while it's ripe, you don't pretend it lasts forever.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she reshapes her business around robots and accepts that it might only last a few years. Family support, especially her mother's, is part of the plan. She's honest that she doesn't know what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Plan, save, learn, build something. Families and communities that work together will come through it better than anyone waiting for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I like ten years. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage close to gone, the kids grown. I could build the firm properly, grow it with the change, and sell it before the end. That's a good life's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the firm in a year or two, as a drone and survey business, then add robots as they arrive. Keep investing a bit every month. Train a couple of young people from the mosque community who need a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the young people from the mosque community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone gave me a start. My first foreman, Ray, took a chance on a woman in a headscarf when others laughed. I'd want to do that for someone else, even if the work only lasts ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What people do with themselves when there's no work. I believe work is good for a person. If nobody needs to work, I worry about the young men on our street with nothing to get up for.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for planning, saving, learning and building, and families and communities that work together will do better than anyone waiting for a handout.
S4.think: I like ten years, since by fifty-three the mortgage would be close to gone and the kids grown. I could build the firm properly, grow it with the change and sell it before the end.
S4.do: Starts a drone and survey firm in a year or two and adds robots as they arrive. Invests monthly and trains young people from her mosque community who need a start.
S4.quote: My first foreman, Ray, took a chance on a woman in a headscarf when others laughed.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she sees a full business cycle she can build and sell. Her urge to give others a start comes from her own first foreman. Her worry turns to the meaning of work for young people, which fits her traditional values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is a slower rollout, so small businesses and families can adjust, and fair rules so the giant companies can't shut out small firms. Help that gets people working, not just paid to stay home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What we tell our children work is for. If the machines do the jobs, we still need to raise people who want to be useful. That's not something a robot will teach them.

headlineQuote: Two years isn't a market, it's a flood.
portrait: Fatima Yilmaz is a 43-year-old overhead lineworker at a city depot who has become her crew's specialist in drone laser scanning, and she uses AI daily for work and family life. Married to Kemal, a self-employed heating engineer, with two children and more than a year of savings, she has been quietly planning her own contracting firm. She's calm in the mild scenarios, where steady change would bring her firm forward. Fast AGI makes her anxious because it kills her plan, while five or ten years let her rebuild the firm around robots, guided by faith, family and her father's business sense.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would sweep away her business plan and leave families and small firms no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A slower rollout, fair rules that stop giant companies shutting out small firms, and help that gets people working rather than paid to stay home.
